questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify a subject open to both levels of government at once
questions.stem: Congress and a state legislature both enact rules about how employers report wages to the government. What allows both to act on the same subject?
questions.explanation: Some subjects are open to both levels at the same time, taxation being the plainest example, and each may act within its own grant, so parallel rules are valid unless one conflicts with the other or the national rule prevails. A shared subject therefore does not mean only one level may legislate, and no clause requires two executives to sign together before either rule has force.
questions.hint: Ask whether the subject is exclusive to one level or open to both.

options.text: A law counts only if both chief executives sign it
options.misconception: invents a joint-signature rule that no clause imposes

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify the clause that leaves a field to the national level alone
questions.stem: A state law charters a bank that issues its own notes and lends money, and Congress objects that no clause gives a state this power. Which constitutional point supports the objection?
questions.explanation: The clauses granting the national level the power to coin money, borrow money on credit, and emit bills of credit leave no room for a state to do the same, so the state charter cannot stand at all. A shared or first-in-time scheme cannot cure that, because the exclusion removes the subject from state reach rather than ranking the two rules against each other.
questions.hint: Is the subject open to both levels, or taken away from the states?

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: state the purpose limit on federal appropriations
questions.stem: Congress funds a programme that builds water systems in several states that flood often. What makes the appropriation constitutional in form?
questions.explanation: The spending clause lets Congress pay out of the treasury to promote the general welfare, and spending that helps a group of states at once meets that test where spending that serves a single private interest would not. Approval by states, a written request, and a geographic limit to the capital are conditions no clause imposes, and a programme subject to none of them still has to clear the purpose test.
questions.hint: The test is about purpose, not about procedure or location.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Powers to lay taxes and duties
questions.learningObjective: identify the clause that supports collecting a duty on imported goods
questions.stem: A resident asks what allows the national government to demand money from importers, and the answer given is a duty on goods brought into the country. Which power is being described?
questions.explanation: Congress may lay and collect taxes, duties, imposts, and excises, and a duty on imported goods is the plainest example, so the clause being used is about raising revenue rather than about spending what has been raised or about the currency in which payment is made. Confusing it with the spend, the commerce power, or the coinage power swaps an unrelated grant for the one actually exercised.
questions.hint: Revenue raising, not revenue spending. Which clause does that?

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify the consent required before two states may bind each other
questions.stem: Two neighbouring states sign an agreement creating a shared water authority, and neither asks the national legislature. Whose consent is needed before the agreement binds them?
questions.explanation: The Constitution provides that no agreement between two states takes effect without the consent of the national legislature, which acts as a check on arrangements that could otherwise draw states into a foreign alliance or a protected commercial monopoly, and a compact is an agreement among sovereigns. Consent, not a referendum or a single officer approval, is what the clause names, and nothing else in the system supplies it.
questions.hint: Which body must say yes before the agreement binds anyone?

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: describe the legal character of money offered to a state
questions.stem: The national government offers a state money for highway maintenance and asks nothing in return if the state accepts. What is the legal character of that offer?
questions.explanation: Money paid to a state for a public purpose is a grant-in-aid, and because the national level gives rather than commands in this posture the state decides whether to take it, so a refusal forfeits the money and nothing else. Treating appropriated funds as an order, an offer as a contract, or a payment as a tax each recasts a voluntary transfer into a legal obligation the state never accepted.
questions.hint: Can a state say no, and what does saying no cost?

options.text: A tax the state may pay or decline, as any taxpayer may

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: apply the limit on federal compulsion of state legislatures
questions.stem: Congress enacts a programme and instructs state legislatures to enact a matching law within a year. Why is that instruction defective?
questions.explanation: Congress may regulate individuals directly and may offer states money for a public purpose, but it may not command a state legislature to enact a law, because a state legislature exercises national power only when the state itself acts. The other readings either deny federal supremacy, hand the compulsion to a branch that does not have it, or imagine an executive signing in place of a state legislature.
questions.hint: A state legislature acts for the state, not for the nation.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a command without payment from an offer of money
questions.stem: A new national rule requires every state to build a records system within two years and offers no money for the work. What kind of instrument is that?
questions.explanation: A rule that orders states to act without paying for the work is an unfunded mandate, and it differs from a grant at exactly the point of compulsion, since a grant is an offer the state may refuse. Calling it a grant, a preemption rule, or a shared power names a different legal device each time, and none of them permits an order to a state that carries no money with it.
questions.hint: The difference between the two is whether the state can refuse.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: apply the legal limits on conditions attached to a federal grant
questions.stem: Congress offers a state a grant for a hospital programme and requires, as a condition of payment, that the state also spend its own money on parts of the same programme. What must the condition satisfy to be enforceable?
questions.explanation: Because Congress pays for the programme it may attach conditions, and the limits on that power are that the conditions must be unambiguous, must relate to the federal interest in the programme, and must not be so forceful that taking the money is the only way to avoid them. Making a condition a matter of state constitutional text, a vote count, or a legislative veto misreads which limits apply to the spending power.
questions.hint: Clarity, connection to the federal purpose, and freedom from compulsion.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a grant a state must direct narrowly from a flexible one
questions.stem: One federal programme requires a state to spend the money on listed purposes only, and another lets a state use the money for any related public purpose. What distinguishes the two?
questions.explanation: A programme limited to listed purposes is closed-ended, and one a state may direct within a broad subject is open-ended, so the difference is how much of the spending decision stays with the state rather than how large the payment is or how long it lasts. Both remain grants a state may decline, which is why treating either as compulsory confuses flexibility with legal obligation.
questions.hint: Look at the spending decision, not at the size or the length.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: apply the limit on direct federal spending on state property
questions.stem: Congress appropriates money to build a new research building on land owned by a state university, over the state objection. What is the obstacle to that plan?
questions.explanation: The spending power reaches the nation own purchases, and putting a federal building on land a state owns would move the state into a position it has not agreed to, so money for a state-owned project generally has to reach the state as funds instead. Confusing this with a geographic limit, a total ban on funds, or a use restriction changes what is being limited and leaves the actual obstacle standing.
questions.hint: The problem is who owns the ground, not where the money goes.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: apply the limit on federal regulation of state personnel affairs
questions.stem: A federal agency adopts a rule about how every employer, state and local governments included, must treat its own staff pay and overtime. Which limit applies to that rule?
questions.explanation: The national level reaches the states through its own enumerated powers, and the power to regulate commerce and the power to tax do not extend to telling a state how to run its own personnel affairs as an employer, which is a function of state sovereignty, though cooperation and taxation still reach states in some ways. Treating the rule as complete power or complete immunity discards a limit that is narrow rather than absolute.
questions.hint: There is a gap here, but it is a narrow one. How wide?

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: State share of a matching grant
questions.learningObjective: compute the state share required by a matching ratio
questions.stem: A federal programme offers a grant of sixty million dollars and requires the state to contribute one dollar for every three the federal government pays. How much must the state spend to obtain the whole grant?
questions.explanation: One state dollar for every three federal dollars makes the state share one quarter of the whole project, so sixty million dollars is three quarters and the remaining quarter is twenty million, giving a total project of eighty million. The tempting answers take the share off the grant instead of the total, invent a dollar-for-dollar match, or divide by four without using the ratio that was given.
questions.hint: The federal part is three quarters of the total, so work out the whole.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: compute a per-capita share of a divided grant
questions.stem: Three states divide a federal grant of six hundred sixty million dollars strictly in proportion to population. Their populations are sixty million, thirty million, and ten million. How much does the smallest state receive?
questions.explanation: The three populations total one hundred million, so the smallest state holds one tenth and takes one tenth of six hundred sixty million, which is sixty-six million. Dividing the money into three even pieces, or assigning the shares by rank instead of by population, ignores the stated rule that population is the only key to the division.
questions.hint: Add the three populations, then take the share that matches.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: compute a shortfall from a two-column budget table
questions.stem: A budget table shows receipts of two thousand one hundred fifty billion dollars and spending of two thousand four hundred eighty billion dollars for one year. What is the shortfall of spending over receipts?
questions.explanation: A shortfall is the excess of spending over receipts, and two thousand four hundred eighty minus two thousand one hundred fifty is three hundred thirty billion dollars. Adding the two columns gives the combined total rather than the gap, and the other figures come from halving or rounding a difference that needs neither operation.
questions.hint: One column minus the other, no rounding needed.

questions.stem: A state budget report shows one billion two hundred million dollars of state-raised spending and three hundred million dollars received from the national government. About what share of all state spending is federal money?
questions.explanation: Total state spending is the sum of the two sources, one billion five hundred million, and federal money is three hundred million of that, which is a fifth, or 20 percent. The 25 percent figure comes from dividing by the state-raised amount alone and answers a different question, and 80 percent is the state own share of the same total, so the arithmetic in two of the four answers describes something real but not what was asked.
questions.hint: Add the two sources first, then take the federal part of the sum.

questions.learningObjective: compute combined growth from two component budgets
questions.stem: A budget office compares two agencies across two years. Agency A rises from four hundred to four hundred sixty million dollars, and agency B stays at two hundred million. About what percent did their combined budget grow?
questions.explanation: The two budgets together rise from six hundred million to six hundred sixty million, so an increase of sixty million on a base of six hundred million is one tenth, or 10 percent. Agency A fifteen percent is real but describes only part of the base, and averaging rates or spreading a single change across two years both distort a comparison between one year and the next.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a study describing an official who holds back appropriated money
questions.stem: An original study describes a department official who holds back money Congress has already appropriated for a programme, on the ground that the agency can administer the work more slowly than the appropriation assumed, and it records that no statute gives the official further authority. What is the best conclusion?
questions.explanation: An appropriation supplies both the legal permission and the ceiling for spending, and once money is appropriated an official may stage or slow the work in some situations but may not simply decide the amount will not be spent, which is what the study describes with no statutory basis offered. Neither executive approval nor administrative prudence supplies the missing authority, and a conclusion of that kind would let any holder of office shrink a voted programme.

questions.topic: A confound in a grant comparison
questions.learningObjective: identify the flaw in a study comparing two grant programmes
questions.stem: An original note compares two states after one adopted a federal grant whose condition required it to keep its own spending at least at a stated level, while the other took a grant with no such condition. The note reports better results in the first state and concludes that the condition caused the improvement. What is the flaw?
questions.explanation: A condition requiring a state to maintain its own spending exists to stop the grant from substituting for state money, so the first state may be spending more of its own, and without holding that constant the better results there could come from state spending rather than from the condition. The note has to report what the first state did with its own money, and the other objections change the question instead of answering the one that was asked.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: describe an arrangement where one level sets the goal and another delivers
questions.stem: A national law sets one standard for how a service must be delivered across the country, and state agencies carry out the work under their own hiring and scheduling rules. What kind of relationship is that?
questions.explanation: When a national law sets the goal and state agencies handle delivery under their own rules, the two levels are working together on a single task, and that arrangement is usually described as cooperative. Calling it competitive, centralised, or judicial removes either the shared administration, the state role, or the statutory standard, and each of those omissions is exactly what makes the relationship what it is.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Tax on the pay of another sovereign
questions.learningObjective: apply the limit on taxing the other sovereign's own people
questions.stem: A state levies an income tax on the pay of federal employees who live in the state. Which limit applies to that state tax?
questions.explanation: Each level taxing power is limited by the other sovereign immunity, so a tax aimed at the pay of the other government own employees is generally forbidden even though the state may tax the income of everyone else living there. The other readings either ignore that limit, overreach by banning the state own income tax, or treat the immunity as something the other level could simply waive on request.
questions.hint: Who is the tax aimed at, rather than where they live?

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: analyze the incentive a matching requirement creates
questions.stem: Two states receive identical block grants and must each provide part of the money from their own budgets. One governor notes that her state must provide a larger share because its own revenue base is smaller. What does this design produce?
questions.explanation: A matching requirement ties part of the federal payment to a state own spending, so a state with a smaller revenue base must commit a larger share of what it can raise, which rewards improving that base and weighs on a low one, and this holds even though the two grants are identical in size. Options describing rewards for cutting or abandoning the programme, or for shrinking revenue capacity, reverse the direction of the incentive.
questions.hint: Which way does the requirement push a state own resources?

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Authority and money as separate steps
questions.learningObjective: explain the difference between authority to run a programme and money for it
questions.stem: A federal programme was created by a statute whose authority has now expired, and a fresh appropriation for the current year is already law. Explain what the programme may do this year, what may not happen without new authority, and what would be needed for it to continue next year.
questions.explanation: A strong answer separates the statute that created the programme from the annual decision to fund it, explains that expired authority removes the legal basis going forward, and then explains why a current appropriation reaches only the period it covers. Answers that treat an appropriation as permanent, or treat expired authority as a bar to money already appropriated, run the two steps together.
questions.hint: Ask what authorises the programme and what authorises the spending.

provenance.author: bank-team-usg-b
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

answer.exemplar: A strong answer separates the two steps in the system: the statute that created the programme supplies the legal authority for it to exist, while the annual appropriation supplies permission to spend money for the period it covers. Since the authority has expired, the programme has no legal basis for anything beyond what current law allows, even though money is available this year, and continuing it next year would require both a new appropriation and fresh authority. An answer that treats the appropriation as permanent, or treats expired authority as a bar to money already lawfully appropriated for this year, merges two steps the system keeps apart.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Declining a grant against honouring it
questions.learningObjective: explain why acceptance and refusal have different legal consequences
questions.stem: Explain why a state may decline to take part in a new federally funded programme but cannot simply walk away from money it has already accepted, and say what the difference turns on.
questions.explanation: A strong answer identifies the offer character of the grant, explains that refusal carries no penalty beyond the money, and then explains that the conditions accepted along with the money continue to bind the state that took it. Answers that treat consent as exhausted at the moment of acceptance, or that call every state role freely revocable, remove the reason the two situations differ.
questions.hint: Compare the position before accepting with the position after.

provenance.author: bank-team-usg-b
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

answer.exemplar: A strong answer explains that a federal grant is an offer, so a state is free to refuse it and lose nothing beyond the money, whereas acceptance places the state inside a relationship whose terms include the conditions attached to the payment, and money already received cannot simply be dropped. The difference therefore turns on the character of the federal instrument as an offer rather than an order, together with what acceptance of the conditions does to the state that has taken the money. Answers that treat acceptance as a one-time consent with no continuing obligations, or that describe every state role as freely revocable, collapse that distinction.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Whose cost a grant programme carries
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a study that understates the cost of a grant programme
questions.stem: An original note reports that a federal grant programme distributes money to every state and concludes that the programme costs the federal budget alone. The note own table shows a matching requirement, state administrative staff time, and in-kind contributions of vehicles and buildings. What should the note conclude?
questions.explanation: The total cost of a programme includes what recipients contribute, not only the payments made, so a matching requirement, staff time, and in-kind contributions all belong in a cost estimate, and reporting only the appropriated amount understates what the programme consumes. Treating the total as purely federal, dividing it evenly without the table, or dismissing the table as irrelevant each misreads what a cost estimate is meant to capture.
questions.hint: Count every contribution to the programme, not only the cheques.
